text: PINNs and neural operators A PINN fits a neural representation of a particular solution; a neural operator learns a map from input functions such as coefficients or initial data to solution functions. Their targets and validation protocols differ. Problem and representative equations A PINN minimizes an empirical weighted loss of PDE, boundary and data residuals. N and B are differential/boundary operators and f,g are prescribed data. A representative FNO layer combines a Fourier-parameterized integral operator K with a local map W acting on feature functions v. Algorithm For a PINN, scale coordinates/units, differentiate residuals, specify collocation points and boundary enforcement, and optimize. FNO trains an operator on input/reference-solution pairs and truncates Fourier modes. Cite the PINN and FNO papers as separate proposals. Conditions and pitfalls Small training loss is not a bound on global solution error or conservation. Examine residual imbalance, shocks, stiff scales and out-of-distribution inputs. Transfer between discretizations is not a guarantee of physical correctness at arbitrary resolution. What to check Compare against analytic or independently converged conventional solutions. Measure off-training L1/L2/L∞ errors, boundaries, conservation and multiple seeds. Split operator data by independent problems rather than nearby time slices alone, and report distribution-shift tests separately.
